sentences.text: This marine reptile possessed large shoulder bones that indicate it was capable of powerful forward strokes for fast swimming.
It likely fed on fish, catching them with its sharp, needle-like teeth.
Thomas Hawkins acquired the remains in the early 1830s from a quarry in Street, Somerset, and described them in 1834.
Charles William Andrews named the genus Eurycleidus in 1922 after re-preparing and exposing the pectoral girdle of the specimen originally known as Plesiosaurus arcuatus.
The genus Eurycleidus contains only one currently accepted species, E. arcuatus.
Most phylogenetic analyses classify Eurycleidus arcuatus as a relatively basal member of the family Rhomaleosauridae.
Eurycleidus lived during the Hettangian to Pliensbachian stages of the Early Jurassic, approximately 201.4 to 184.2 million years ago.

It is debated whether E. megacephalus belongs to Eurycleidus; while Smith (2007) reassigned it to the genus, most analyses suggest it represents a distinct, unnamed genus separate from Eurycleidus and Rhomaleosaurus.
A specimen from Halberstadt, Germany, originally assigned to Eurycleidus arcuatus, was moved to the distinct genus Lindwurmia in 2019.
